explanations.answer: The Day of the LORD's anger
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Zephaniah stacks up his hurry-ups, and the last one says “…before the Day of the LORD’s anger comes upon you.” (Zephaniah 2:2) He also says the day passes “like chaff,” which is light stuff that blows away. So he isn't pointing at a party. He's pointing at a day that's coming.

No crown and no parade in this verse, friend. The prophet's hurry is about “the Day of the LORD’s anger.” (Zephaniah 2:2) A coronation you can show up late to, but this day is different. Zephaniah wants them gathered before it arrives.

A festival would be a nice change of pace, but it isn't in the verse. Zephaniah talks about “the burning anger of the LORD” and “the Day of the LORD’s anger.” (Zephaniah 2:2) That's no calendar event with snacks on the table. It's a day you want to be ready for.

There it is: “Seek the LORD, all you humble of the earth who carry out His justice.” (Zephaniah 2:3) Then he adds two more, “Seek righteousness; seek humility.” Nobody is told to go find a hiding spot first. I think the whole point is to go toward Him.

Running for the hills sounds sensible, I'll give you that. But Zephaniah never says it here. He says “Seek the LORD, all you humble of the earth who carry out His justice.” (Zephaniah 2:3) The direction he gives is toward the LORD, not away from town.

Walls would keep a lot of folks busy, but they aren't in this verse. The humble are told to “Seek the LORD,” and then to “Seek righteousness; seek humility.” (Zephaniah 2:3) No bricks, no trowels, no scaffolding. Just seeking.

Careful, friend, because this one sounds so nice you want to say yes. But the verse says, “Perhaps you will be sheltered on the day of the LORD’s anger.” (Zephaniah 2:3) “Perhaps” is not “surely.” The text leaves it open, so I leave it open too.

You caught the little word. The verse says “Perhaps you will be sheltered on the day of the LORD’s anger.” (Zephaniah 2:3) A promise would say surely, and Zephaniah doesn't. So the humble are told to seek, and they seek with everything they've got.

Yes, “Gaza will be abandoned, and Ashkelon left in ruins.” (Zephaniah 2:4) Abandoned means the people are gone. Picture a kitchen with every cookie sheet hauled off and nobody left to flip the oven on. That's the first city on his list.

Rebuilt would be good news for Gaza, but the verse goes the other way. Ashkelon is “left in ruins,” and Gaza “will be abandoned.” (Zephaniah 2:4) Nobody is hauling bricks back in on this line. The ruins stay ruins.

Spared is a hopeful word, friend, but it doesn't show up here. The verse says Gaza “will be abandoned” and Ashkelon is “left in ruins.” (Zephaniah 2:4) No dodging and no last minute pardon on that list. Zephaniah says it plainly.

Zephaniah spells it out: “O Canaan, land of the Philistines.” (Zephaniah 2:5) So the word of the LORD is against the Philistines' land on that seacoast. He names the Cherethites in the same breath. The verse doesn't leave you guessing.

The Edomites, Esau's descendants (Genesis 36:9), don't show up in this verse. The text says “O Canaan, land of the Philistines.” (Zephaniah 2:5) Easy to mix up when a list of nations is rolling. Keep your eye on the seacoast.

The Midianites aren't in this verse. Zephaniah says “O Canaan, land of the Philistines.” (Zephaniah 2:5) He's pointing at the seacoast, not at some other neighbor. So the answer sits right there in the line.

True. “So the seacoast will become a land of pastures, with wells for shepherds and folds for sheep.” (Zephaniah 2:6) A coastline full of cities turns into a place for shepherds. They get wells, and the sheep get folds.

Plot twist, friend, it's actually true. The verse says the seacoast “will become a land of pastures, with wells for shepherds and folds for sheep.” (Zephaniah 2:6) The line before has the LORD saying “no one will be left.” I'd have guessed rubble forever, but the text says pastures.

That's it: “The coast will belong to the remnant of the house of Judah.” (Zephaniah 2:7) A remnant is the ones who are left. So the coast ends up with the leftover folks from Judah's house. And they find pasture there.

Egypt's armies aren't anywhere in this verse. The text says the coast “will belong to the remnant of the house of Judah.” (Zephaniah 2:7) That's the group Zephaniah names. Nobody marches in with a banner.
Traders would make sense on a coast, I'll give you that. But the verse gives it to “the remnant of the house of Judah.” (Zephaniah 2:7) Tyre isn't mentioned at all. The text gives you the answer.

True. They “will lie down in the evening among the houses of Ashkelon.” (Zephaniah 2:7) That's the same Ashkelon that was “left in ruins” back in verse 4. Now there are folks lying down there at sundown, and that's quite a switch.

This one is actually true, friend. The text says they “will lie down in the evening among the houses of Ashkelon.” (Zephaniah 2:7) Ashkelon was “left in ruins” in verse 4, and now it has company at sundown. It's a quiet picture after some loud verses.

Yes, “for the LORD their God will attend to them and restore their captives.” (Zephaniah 2:7) Restore is a word I'm fond of. I sat dusty and forgotten in a junk drawer myself before I was called out of it. So when I hear about captives being restored, I perk right up.

Scatter is the opposite of what the verse says. The LORD “will attend to them and restore their captives.” (Zephaniah 2:7) Attending means He looks after them. So the captives are on the receiving end of good news.

Selling is what you'd do with a pile of old kitchen gadgets, not what the verse says. Here the LORD “will attend to them and restore their captives.” (Zephaniah 2:7) The captives come back instead. That's a very different ending.

The LORD says Moab and the Ammonites “have taunted My people and threatened their borders.” (Zephaniah 2:8) So it wasn't only words, it was edging toward their land. Think of a neighbor who keeps drifting over to your side of the fence. That's not a friendly wave.

The temple isn't named in this verse. The LORD says they “have taunted My people and threatened their borders.” (Zephaniah 2:8) The threat was aimed at the edges of the land. So the temple answer doesn't fit this line.

Harvest sounds like it could fit, but it isn't what the verse says. The LORD says they “have taunted My people and threatened their borders.” (Zephaniah 2:8) Borders are the lines around the land. Nothing about crops is mentioned here.

The LORD says, “surely Moab will be like Sodom and the Ammonites like Gomorrah.” (Zephaniah 2:9) Sodom and Gomorrah were the cities where the LORD rained down sulfur and fire (Genesis 19:24). So the picture is a place left empty. Everybody in Zephaniah's day knew those two names.

Jericho and Ai are cities from Joshua's story (Joshua 6:20; Joshua 8:28), but the LORD names a different pair. He says, “surely Moab will be like Sodom and the Ammonites like Gomorrah.” (Zephaniah 2:9) Those are the two cities He uses as the picture. Don't let the other names pull you off.

Tyre and Sidon are cities Jesus names in Matthew 11:21, but not here. In Zephaniah the LORD says, “surely Moab will be like Sodom and the Ammonites like Gomorrah.” (Zephaniah 2:9) So the pair is Sodom and Gomorrah. Easy to mix up when city names are flying around.
True. “The remnant of My people will plunder them; the remainder of My nation will dispossess them.” (Zephaniah 2:9) The LORD names His own people's remnant for the job. Two lines, same message.

This one is actually true, friend. The LORD says, “The remnant of My people will plunder them; the remainder of My nation will dispossess them.” (Zephaniah 2:9) It's right there in the verse. So the remnant is the one doing the plundering.

Yes, “This they shall have in return for their pride, for taunting and mocking the people of the LORD of Hosts.” (Zephaniah 2:10) Pride is the word the verse uses. It's joined with taunting and mocking. Pride is what the LORD names.

Poverty isn't in this verse. The LORD says they get this “in return for their pride, for taunting and mocking the people of the LORD of Hosts.” (Zephaniah 2:10) The word He uses is pride. So what they're repaid for has nothing to do with being poor.

Fear isn't the word in this verse. It says, “in return for their pride, for taunting and mocking the people of the LORD of Hosts.” (Zephaniah 2:10) People who taunt and mock aren't usually the scared ones. Pride is the word the text gives.

That's the finish of the verse: “Then the nations of every shore will bow in worship to Him, each in its own place.” (Zephaniah 2:11) Each nation does it in its own place. So it's not one big crowd in one spot. It's every shore.

The verse goes the opposite direction. It says, “Then the nations of every shore will bow in worship to Him, each in its own place.” (Zephaniah 2:11) Bowing, not rising up. The LORD “will be terrifying” to them, and the nations end up bowing.

Hiding sounds likely after the word “terrifying,” but that's not where the verse lands. It says, “Then the nations of every shore will bow in worship to Him, each in its own place.” (Zephaniah 2:11) The nations bow in worship. It's out in the open, shore by shore.
Yes, “And He will stretch out His hand against the north and destroy Assyria.” (Zephaniah 2:13) Right after that comes Nineveh. The verse names the nation first and then the city.

Egypt isn't named in this verse. Zephaniah says the LORD will “stretch out His hand against the north and destroy Assyria.” (Zephaniah 2:13) The name the text gives is Assyria. Keep your eye on the north.

Edom doesn't appear in this verse. The text says the LORD will “stretch out His hand against the north and destroy Assyria.” (Zephaniah 2:13) So the nation is Assyria. Nineveh is named in the next line.
True. “He will make Nineveh a desolation, as dry as a desert.” (Zephaniah 2:13) Dry as a desert is a big drop for a great city. That's the verse as it's written.
This one is true, friend. The verse says, “He will make Nineveh a desolation, as dry as a desert.” (Zephaniah 2:13) Those are the words Zephaniah uses. So the answer is True.
Yes. “Herds will lie down in her midst, creatures of every kind.” (Zephaniah 2:14) The desert owl and the screech owl roost on her pillars. Not a crowd that pays rent.

Merchants would at least bring in some business, but the verse never says so. It says, “Herds will lie down in her midst, creatures of every kind.” (Zephaniah 2:14) And owls take the pillars. No shops are opening.

No soldiers or kings in this verse. Zephaniah says, “Herds will lie down in her midst, creatures of every kind,” and the owls roost “atop her pillars.” (Zephaniah 2:14) The ones who move in are animals. Nobody important.

explanations.answer: That no one else compares to her
explanations.explanation: Yes, she thinks to herself, “I am it, and there is none besides me.” (Zephaniah 2:15) That's a city telling itself there's no one else like her. Zephaniah calls her a “carefree city that dwells securely.” Nobody who thinks that way is shopping for help.
Allies aren't on her mind in this verse. She thinks, “I am it, and there is none besides me.” (Zephaniah 2:15) A city that says that isn't looking around for help. She thinks she's all anyone needs.

Her days being numbered would be a worried thought, and she doesn't have one. The verse says she thinks, “I am it, and there is none besides me.” (Zephaniah 2:15) That's the opposite of worried. She's carefree, remember?
The verse says the opposite, friend. “Everyone who passes by her hisses and shakes his fist.” (Zephaniah 2:15) Nobody stops to weep. They hiss and shake a fist as they go by.
Yes, no weeping. The verse says, “Everyone who passes by her hisses and shakes his fist.” (Zephaniah 2:15) Passersby hiss and shake a fist. That's how the text says people treat the ruined city.
